    Single-frame Mean-Shift Super-Resolution

    Source: R/mssr.R
    mssr.Rd

    Computes the Mean-Shift Super-Resolution (MSSR) structure map of one 2D frame (Torres-Garcia et al. 2022). The result is a structural map for display, structure analysis or mask derivation. It is not a quantitative intensity: MSSR is nonlinear, suppresses dim structures next to bright ones and can hollow or split broad objects. Take measurements from the original data (see mssr_mask()).

    Usage

    mssr(
  x,
  fwhm,
  amp = 1L,
  order = 1L,
  intensity_normalize = TRUE,
  mesh = TRUE,
  grid = c("extent", "endpoint"),
  kernel = c("disk", "square"),
  rounding = c("half_even", "half_up"),
  max_output_pixels = 5e+07,
  max_memory_bytes = NULL
)

    Arguments

    x

    A plain integer or double matrix (rows = y, columns = x) with finite values and no explicit class. Input dimnames and other attributes are discarded; acquisition metadata are never inferred from attributes.

    fwhm

    Full width at half maximum of the point-spread function, in input pixels. Required; there is no default because it is a property of the acquisition. Prefer a measured PSF: a theoretical value such as 0.51 * wavelength / NA (emission wavelength, divided by the pixel size) describes an ideal widefield system, and aberrations, defocus and pixel size can widen the recorded PSF. Under noise an fwhm below the true PSF makes false peaks more likely, while a larger one gives a shallower dip between close sources; when unsure, choose the larger plausible value. Only the kernel half-size, 0.5 * fwhm * amp rounded as set by rounding and at least 1 (recorded in parameters$half_size), enters the computation, so nearby values can give identical results.

    amp

    Amplification factor (whole number from 1 to 64).

    order

    MSSR order (whole number from 0 to 10). Orders above 3 are experimental: bounded high-precision checks found larger errors at order 10. They emit mssrscopR_warning_unqualified_order. Checks at orders 0 through 3 cover only the documented synthetic domain, not every input.

    intensity_normalize

    If TRUE (the authors' default) the structure map is multiplied by the (amplified) input.

    mesh

    Mesh compensation after amplification (only used if amp > 1).

    grid

    "extent" (field-of-view-preserving, default) or "endpoint" (samples from the first to the last input pixel center, as the authors' code does; for comparison only).

    kernel

    Neighborhood shape: "disk" (authors' R code) or "square" (authors' Python code).

    rounding

    Rounding of the kernel half-size 0.5 * fwhm * amp: "half_even" (R and Python default) or "half_up".

    max_output_pixels

    Upper limit on output pixels, checked before any computation.

    max_memory_bytes

    Optional positive allocation-estimate ceiling. NULL leaves this guard disabled. This is not a hard process-memory cap; see mssr_estimate_resources().

    Value

    An object of class mssr_result: a list with values (numeric matrix), role ("structure" or "intensity_weighted_structure"), transform, parameters, engine and diagnostics. transform holds amp, grid, input_dim, output_dim, the first output pixel center and the spacing (input-pixel units), and field_of_view: the input frame's extent from pixel edge 0.5 to n + 0.5. Output samples cover it exactly on the extent grid; on the endpoint grid they span only the first to the last input pixel center. The input is not stored. schema_version identifies the result contract separately from the numerical engine; input records known axes and unknown calibration; evidence identifies the numerical-only scope. Qualification diagnostics disclose conservative high-order limits without assigning confidence.

    Details

    Geometry. The output keeps the input orientation. With grid = "extent" the amplified grid preserves the field of view: output pixel centers lie at (k - 0.5) / amp + 0.5 input pixels, so the spacing is exactly 1 / amp. Amplification adds samples, not independent observations.

    Relation to the authors' code. At amp = 1 with intensity_normalize = FALSE, tested non-degenerate examples agree with the authors' single-frame R function after its final 90-degree rotation is undone (kernel = "disk") or their Python function (kernel = "square") within floating-point tolerance. Extreme numeric ranges and undefined refinement steps can differ (see below). For amp > 1, mssr() uses the supplement's cubic kernel (Keys cubic convolution, a = -1/2). The authors' R script interpolates with akima's Akima method and their Python script with a SciPy spline, and their R mesh shifts asymmetrically, so the amplified input already differs beyond rounding; MSSR's range normalization and refinement are nonlinear and can enlarge such differences locally. Do not expect pixel-wise agreement with their amplified maps, even with grid = "endpoint", which reproduces their sample positions. With the default intensity_normalize = TRUE their R function multiplies the rotated map by the unrotated input, so it agrees with mssr() only for frames that a 90-degree rotation leaves unchanged (and fails for non-square frames).

    Several channels or bands. mssr() processes one 2D frame. Applied to each channel or band of multichannel or spectral data, it gives every channel its own nonlinear structure map, scaled by that channel's maxima. Intensity-weighted outputs (the default) are guaranteed to keep the channels' intensity ratios only when one whole frame, background included, is a scaled copy of another; a different background or another object elsewhere in the frame can change the ratios, and the structure maps (intensity_normalize = FALSE) of scaled copies are identical. So do not compare channels, form ratios or indices, or assemble spectra from the outputs; measure them on the original data.

    Degenerate input. A flat frame, a frame whose amplified maximum is not positive, a frame without any positive mean shift and a refinement step that leaves no positive value (possible only with signed input) return zeros with diagnostics$degenerate = TRUE and a degenerate_reason. A refinement step (order >= 1) is undefined when the mean-shift map already equals the normalized input, for example for isolated impulses on an exactly zero background. Such a step leaves the map unchanged, is counted in diagnostics$order_steps_skipped and gives a warning of class mssrscopR_warning_skipped_steps: the result is not the limit for slightly perturbed input, because any positive background makes the step defined and changes the map. The authors' R function returns NaN in all of these cases; their Python function returns zeros, which equals mssr() for the degenerate frames but not for skipped refinement steps.

    Negative values and background. MSSR assumes non-negative intensities. Negative input gives a warning of class mssrscopR_warning_negative, and intensity-weighted output can then be negative. Non-negative input is not free of offset effects either: the order-0 structure map (intensity_normalize = FALSE) does not change with a constant background, but every refinement step (order >= 1) compares the map with the input divided by its maximum, which a background changes, and intensity weighting multiplies by the input. Subtracting a background is therefore a preprocessing choice that changes the result; record it with the result. The range normalizer adapts to the largest local difference at each pixel, so even rounding-level ripple on an otherwise flat frame is stretched to full contrast: only an exactly flat frame is degenerate.

    Numeric domain. Input and numeric parameters must use plain integer or double storage, without explicit classes. Convert calibrated or other classed data deliberately before calling. The engine uses internal power-of-two scaling, centered interpolation for non-negative input and weighted local differences to limit overflow, underflow and cancellation. A nonzero input lost during scaling or an overflowing final result raises mssrscopR_error_numerical. Rounding already present in the supplied data cannot be recovered. Intensity-weighted output is rescaled to the original numeric units but remains non-quantitative; subnormal output still has limited precision and can round to zero.

    Cost. Every order step uses image-wide maxima, so frames must be processed whole. Time grows with the number of output pixels times the number of neighborhood offsets (about pi * h^2 for the disk kernel and (2 * h + 1)^2 - 1 for the square kernel, with half-size h, recorded in parameters$half_size). Calls whose estimated work exceeds 1e10 operations, whose output exceeds max_output_pixels, or whose kernel half-size exceeds 1000 pixels are refused before computing.

    References

    Torres-Garcia E, Pinto-Camara R, Linares A, et al. Extending resolution within a single imaging frame. Nature Communications 2022;13:7452. doi:10.1038/s41467-022-34693-9

    See also

    mssr_coords(), mssr_mask(), mssr_selftest()

    Examples

    # Two point sources 3 pixels apart, blurred with FWHM 3 px.
g <- expand.grid(r = 1:21, c = 1:25)
spot <- function(r0, c0) exp(-((g$r - r0)^2 + (g$c - c0)^2) / (2 * (3 / 2.3548)^2))
x <- matrix(spot(11, 11) + spot(11, 14) + 0.05, 21, 25)
res <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
res
#> <mssr_result> intensity_weighted_structure
#>   input 21 x 25 -> output 42 x 50 (amp 2, extent grid)
#>   fwhm 3 px, order 1, kernel disk (half-size 3), mesh TRUE
#>   engine mssr_r_rev3; zero fraction 0.498
#>   Not a quantitative intensity: measure on the original data.
dim(as.matrix(res))
#> [1] 42 50
